arXiv:2607.28418v1 [cs.AI] 30 Jul 2026

WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning

Haozhe Hu Hao Wu Peiran Yin Chao Han Yunpu Ma Xiaoyu Shen ††thanks: Corresponding Author Affiliation: Ningbo Institute of Digital Twin, Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning, LMU Munich Hhz029@hotmail.com; xyshen@eitech.edu.cn
Abstract

Pruning is a promising approach for improving the efficiency of large language models (LLMs). Existing static structured pruning methods are hardware-friendly and can deliver practical throughput gains, but their input-agnostic computation allocation often causes substantial accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity. Recent dynamic sparsity methods improve quality retention by adapting computation to individual inputs, yet they remain largely limited to coarse-grained structural decisions and their practical acceleration under real-world inference scenarios remains challenging. To address these challenges, we present WIDE, the first end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework designed for both prefill and decode scenarios. WIDE enables fine-grained computation allocation by allowing each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, extending dynamic pruning beyond layer-level decisions to neuron-block-level granularity. Through a two-stage training pipeline, WIDE learns effective token-wise sparse execution patterns and achieves substantially better quality retention than existing approaches. To make such fine-grained dynamic pruning practical, we further propose a pruning–kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, enabling efficient execution across different granularities. At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides 55.1% performance boost when compared to the state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. Under prefill and decoding inference workloads, WIDE achieves close-to-theoretical kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, as well as 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration. These results establish WIDE as an effective fine-grained dynamic width pruning framework that pushes the frontier of token-wise dynamic structured pruning. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LLM-Pruning/tree/main/WIDE.

1 Introduction

The rapid advancement of LLMs has enabled their widespread deployment across a broad range of real-world applications (Team et al., 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2026; Meng et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). However, as model continue to scale and increasingly complex agent harness systems emerge, the efficient LLM serving has become increasingly challenging. Beyond system-level and hardware-specific optimizations (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024; Zadouri et al., 2026), model pruning has also evolved rapidly as a model-level approach to improving inference efficiency. By removing redundant structures along the depth and width dimensions, pruning reduces model size and computational cost, thereby offering a complementary path toward efficient LLM/VLM serving (Cheng et al., 2024; Frantar and Alistarh, 2023; Ma et al., 2023; Ashkboos et al., 2023; Men et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026b; Wu et al., 2026a).

Currently, LLM pruning is dominated by static schemes, which remove predefined structures such as entire layers (Kim et al., 2024), attention or feed-forward network (FFN) sublayers (Zhong et al., 2025), rows or columns of weight matrices (Li et al., 2025), and individual neurons (Fang et al., 2024). Once calibrated, these units are permanently removed, making static pruning simple to deploy and compatible with existing hardware backends. However, applying the same pruning decisions to every input often sacrifices model quality, especially under aggressive sparsity. Dynamic pruning addresses this limitation by introducing lightweight routers that allocate computation according to individual tokens (Raposo et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Han et al., 2025). Despite their improved flexibility, existing dynamic pruning methods primarily operate at the depth level, deciding whether each token should execute or skip entire layers or submodules. Such coarse-grained decisions limit the achievable quality–efficiency trade-off, as tokens that require only partial computation within a layer may still lose useful capacity when the entire module is removed (Shrestha et al., 2025; Gautam et al., 2026). Meanwhile, pushing dynamic pruning toward finer-grained token-wise allocation introduces additional system challenges: irregular execution patterns can prevent the reduced computation from translating into practical inference acceleration (He et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026). Therefore, two fundamental questions remain: (1) Can dynamic pruning move beyond coarse-grained depth decisions to achieve finer computation allocation and better quality retention? (2) Can such fine-grained dynamic decisions be efficiently executed to deliver real end-to-end speedups?

Motivated by these challenges, we present WIDE, the first end-to-end token-wise dynamic width pruning framework that jointly optimizes pruning granularity and GPU execution. WIDE pushes dynamic pruning beyond layer- and sublayer-level routing by enabling each token to independently select fine-grained groups of attention heads and FFN channels. Specifically, lightweight bottleneck routers select group-query-attention (GQA)-aligned attention-head groups and configurable FFN-channel groups independently for every token. The differentiable router-only calibration learns these decisions with end-to-end training, with an optional LoRA recovery (Hu et al., 2021) further restores quality. The group size explicitly controls the trade-off between allocation flexibility and kernel efficiency. To translate these fine-grained decisions into practical acceleration, WIDE further introduces a unified GPU acceleration framework through pruning–kernel co-design. Instead of explicitly materializing token-specific sparse tensors, WIDE first performs mask reordering to transform arbitrary token-wise routing patterns into structured execution layouts. Active tokens from each routing group are packed into tile-aligned prefixes, converting irregular sparsity into CTA-level regularity. Based on this representation, WIDE kernels progressively eliminate unnecessary computation at multiple granularities: hardware-agnostic predicates remove fully inactive CTAs, while architecture-aware predicates further skip inactive memory-loading packets and tensor-core computation fragments. This design enables fine-grained dynamic sparsity to preserve efficient GPU execution patterns and deliver real acceleration for both prefill and decoding workloads.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

(1) We introduce WIDE, the first end-to-end token-wise dynamic pruning framework that achieves fine-grained width-level computation allocation. Unlike previous dynamic pruning approaches that perform token-wise decisions at the layer or sublayer level, WIDE enables each token to dynamically select fine-grained attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups within each Transformer block. This pushes dynamic pruning beyond coarse structural skipping toward neuron-block-level computation allocation, providing substantially finer-grained control over model capacity while maintaining structured GPU execution.
(2) We present the first unified framework that unlocks practical acceleration for fine-grained dynamic sparsity. We identify synchronized mask-to-index conversion and irregular gather–scatter execution as two key obstacles preventing dynamic sparsity from yielding practical speedups. We thus introduce standalone mask-reordering preprocessing together with multi-stage intra-block predication, allowing the resulting kernels to approach the ideal speedup of the prunable operations in both prefill and decoding.
(3) We advance the pruning Pareto frontier through pruning–kernel co-design. To the best of our knowledge, WIDE is the first framework to combine token-wise dynamic width pruning with GPU kernel co-design for both prefill and decoding. At a 50% target sparsity, WIDE improves average zero-shot accuracy by up to 20.26 points over the strongest evaluated dynamic-depth baseline and achieves end-to-end speedups of 1.68×\times and 1.55×\times for prefill and decoding, respectively. The kernel-level analysis also demonstrate up to 200x speedup and 1,000x peak memory reduction compared to naive gather–scatter baselines.

2 Related Works

Static Pruning

Among existing pruning methods, static pruning remains the dominant. Given a small set of calibration samples, these methods estimate the importance of predefined units, such as Transformer layers, attention or FFN sublayers, attention heads, rows or columns of weight matrices, and individual neurons, and permanently remove low-importance units until the target sparsity is reached. According to the pruning unit, existing work can be broadly categorized into depth and width pruning. Depth pruning removes computation along the layer dimension: Shortened LLaMA prunes complete Transformer blocks using perplexity-based or Taylor and heuristic-based importance followed by retraining (Kim et al., 2024); BlockPruner further evaluates attention and FFN residual blocks separately with calibration perplexity (Zhong et al., 2025); recent CoopPruner models layers as interacting players and estimates their marginal contributions with surrogate-assisted Shapley values (Ding et al., 2025). Width pruning instead removes channels, neurons, or attention heads within layers. Representative methods include SliceGPT, which exploits orthogonal invariance and PCA on calibration activations (Ashkboos et al., 2023); Týr-the-Pruner, which searches for a global non-uniform sparsity allocation over FFN channels and attention heads (Li et al., 2025); and recent Deterministic Differentiable Pruning (DDP) (Huang et al., 2026), which learns deterministic structured masks under an ℓ0\ell_{0} sparsity constraint via augmented Lagrangian optimization, avoiding stochastic mask sampling and its train–test mismatch. Beyond structural pruning, methods like SparseGPT Frantar and Alistarh (2023), Wanda Sun et al. (2023), and MaskLLM Fang et al. (2024) further incorporate semi-structured or unstructured masks to individually pruning each neuron. These static methods are deployment-friendly, but their input-agnostic pruning decisions limit their ability to allocate computation adaptively across tokens.

Dynamic Pruning

Dynamic pruning allocates computation adaptively during inference instead of permanently removing a fixed set of parameters. Existing methods mainly focus on token-wise depth or sublayer routing. Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) routes only the top-kk tokens through each Transformer layer under a fixed compute budget (Raposo et al., 2024). D-LLM equips layers with dynamic decision modules to determine whether each token should execute or skip a network unit, together with a KV-cache eviction policy for skipped tokens (Jiang et al., 2024). SkipGPT further decouple attention and FFN modules, using a differentiable routing mechanism to construct a two-stage training Zhao et al. (2025). Informed Routing relaxes binary execute-or-skip decisions by predicting unit outputs with a lightweight feature forecaster (LFF) and thus construct a three-stage recovering (Han et al., 2025). PolarSparse and FastForward instead introduce the dynamic width pruning for batch decode / prefill only (Gautam et al., 2026; Shrestha et al., 2025). While these methods improve adaptive computation, they mostly operate at coarse granularity or specific scenario; WIDE instead studies fine-grained dynamic width pruning and couples its routing design with GPU-oriented block skipping.

3 WIDE: Preliminary, Training, and Inference Design

As previously introduced, WIDE is a dynamic width pruning framework that selectively activates attention head groups and weight matrix blocks under token-wise routing. In this section, we first elaborate on the minimal atomic pruning unit of WIDE, then followed by its two-stage training pipeline, and the customized acceleration framework for dynamic pruning.

3.1 Preliminary

Consider a standard Transformer layer with input token embeddings X∈ℝB×T×D\textbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times D} with BB for batch size, TT for token length, and DD for hidden size, WIDE follows the granularity of SkipGPT (Zhao et al., 2025), which decomposes the entire layer into two computation parts: attention and FFN, with TqT_{q}, TkT_{k} denotes the token length of query and key value, HqH_{q}, HkH_{k} denotes the number of query / key value attention heads, d=DHqd=\frac{D}{H_{q}} denotes the head size, and D′D^{\prime} denotes the intermediate size of FFN’s up scaling. The overall pruning granularity of WIDE is shown in Figure 1, where each token allocates their computation budget based on the atomic pruning group size GG.

Attention Pruning Unit

For the attention layer, considering the compatibility with the standard FlashAttention tiling scheme that launches over BB, HqH_{q}, TqT_{q} dimensions and consumes one head at each step (Dao, 2023), we assume the head as the minimal pruning atom to skip dd or multiple-dd under each token routing. Such pruning strategy can be equivalently represented with a structured mask of the form like:

[Q,K,V]=[X​𝐖q⊤,X​𝐖k⊤,X​𝐖v⊤]\displaystyle[\textbf{Q},\textbf{K},\textbf{V}]=[\textbf{X}\mathbf{W}_{q}^{\top},\textbf{X}\mathbf{W}_{k}^{\top},\textbf{X}\mathbf{W}_{v}^{\top}] (1)
X′=(Attn.​(Q,K,V)⏟ℝB×Tq×Hq×d⊙Gℳattn)​𝐖o⊤where​ℳattn∈{0,1}B×Tq×Hk,G=DHk=HqHk×d\displaystyle\textbf{X}^{\prime}=\left(\underbrace{\text{Attn.}(\textbf{Q},\textbf{K},\textbf{V})}_{\mathbb{R}^{B\times T_{q}\times H_{q}\times d}}\odot_{G}\mathcal{M}_{\text{attn}}\right)\mathbf{W}_{o}^{\top}\quad\text{where}\ \mathcal{M}_{\text{attn}}\in\{0,1\}^{B\times T_{q}\times H_{k}},\ G=\frac{D}{H_{k}}=\frac{H_{q}}{H_{k}}\times d (2)

Here ⊙G\odot_{G} represents to apply gating based on group size. The outer mask ℳattn\mathcal{M}_{\text{attn}} also prevent to pruning over 𝐖k\mathbf{W}_{k} and 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v}, which can lead to cache eviction. Additionally, since that recent LLMs predominantly adopt GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023), WIDE sets attention’s GG to the head group size HqHk×d\frac{H_{q}}{H_{k}}\times d for preserving compatibility with existing GQA decoding optimizations (e.g., XQA (NVIDIA, 2026; Ye et al., 2025)) while minimizing the degradation of pruning flexibility.

FFN Pruning Unit

Unlike attention layers, FFN layers comprise only consecutive general matrix multiplication (GEMM) and element-wise operations. For a standard GEMM operation with its left-hand-side operand (LHS) A∈ℝM×K\textbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times K} and right-hand-side operand (RHS) B∈ℝN×K\textbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times K}, the tiling strategy typically slices all three logical dimensions MM, NN, and KK, with tile sizes (B​M,B​N,B​K)∈𝒯3,𝒯={2k∣k∈ℤ⩾4}.(BM,BN,BK)\in\mathcal{T}^{3},\quad\mathcal{T}=\{2^{k}\mid k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 4}\}. Based on this, WIDE adopts commonly used tiling sizes as the GG for FFN to prune the intermediate dimension D′D^{\prime} into contiguous group. This dimension corresponds to the out-feature in Up/Gate projections and the in-feature in Down projections, ensuring a single mask matrix to represent the entire FFN layer pruning:

X′=((ϕ⁡(X​𝐖gate⊤)⊙(X​𝐖up⊤))⏟ℝB×T×(D′/G,G)⊙Gℳffn)​𝐖down⊤where​ℳffn∈{0,1}B×T×D′G,G∈𝒯\displaystyle\textbf{X}^{\prime}=\left(\underbrace{(\phi(\textbf{X}\mathbf{W}_{\text{gate}}^{\top})\odot(\textbf{X}\mathbf{W}_{\text{up}}^{\top}))}_{\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times(D^{\prime}/G,G)}}\odot_{G}\mathcal{M}_{\text{ffn}}\right)\mathbf{W}_{\text{down}}^{\top}\quad\text{where}\ \mathcal{M}_{\text{ffn}}\in\{0,1\}^{B\times T\times\frac{D^{\prime}}{G}},\ G\in\mathcal{T} (3)

where ϕ\phi denotes element-wise activation function. The GG in FFN unit provides a more flexible choice than attention unit. As GEMM instructions typically support minimum block widths of 16, the available choices for GG lie in the same tiling-size set 𝒯\mathcal{T}, with a trade-off between pruning performance (G↓G\downarrow) and potential acceleration gain (G↑G\uparrow).

Routing Components

Based on the pruning units and their corresponding mask representations described above, we can design the router component for WIDE, which maps the input activation to NGN_{G} binary decisions. To flexibly handle varying dimensions and make compatible with Gumbel Softmax sampling during training, WIDE employs a bottleneck architecture, with the router implementations for attention/FFN layers defined as follows:

ℛ∈ℝB×T×NG×2=reshape⁡(XW1​W2)where​W1∈ℝD×r,W2∈ℝr×2​NG\displaystyle\mathcal{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times N_{G}\times 2}=\operatorname{reshape}\left(\textbf{X}\textbf{W}_{1}\textbf{W}_{2}\right)\quad\text{where}\ \textbf{W}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times r},\ \textbf{W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times 2N_{G}} (4)
ℳ={[argmaxc∈{0,1}ℛ…,c=0],when inference,GumbelSoftmaxτhard​(ℛ)…,0,when training,\displaystyle\mathcal{M}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\text{argmax}_{c\in\{0,1\}}\mathcal{R}_{\ldots,c}=0\right],&\text{when inference},\\ \operatorname{GumbelSoftmax}_{\tau}^{\text{hard}}(\mathcal{R})_{\ldots,0},&\text{when training},\end{cases} (5)

where τ\tau is the temperature, NGN_{G} is set to D/GD/G for attention, and D′/GD^{\prime}/G for FFN. Here r≪Dr\ll D is typically chosen from {16,32}\{16,32\}. In each output pair, class 00 denotes execution and class 11 denotes skipping.

3.2 Two-stage Training

To fully unlock the potential of WIDE, a two-stage training pipeline is introduced to restore model’s original performance. During the first stage that called Router training, all parameters except the router remain frozen, with calibration data employed only to optimize the routing components. In the next optional LoRA tuning stage, LoRA are incorporated into all base models’ linear modules at each layer to further support performance recovery. Both stages utilize not only the standard language modeling loss but also an auxiliary sparsity loss to ensure the pruning meets the target sparsity. For a model with NN layers, the overall objective is similar to SkipGPT:

ℒ=ℒLM+α​|S−12​N​∑i=1N((1−1|ℳattni|​∑ℳattni)+(1−1|ℳffni|​∑ℳffni))|\displaystyle\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}+\alpha\left\lvert S-\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\left(1-\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{M}_{\text{attn}}^{i}\rvert}\sum\mathcal{M}_{\text{attn}}^{i}\right)+\left(1-\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{M}_{\text{ffn}}^{i}\rvert}\sum\mathcal{M}_{\text{ffn}}^{i}\right)\right)\right\rvert (6)

where α\alpha is a hyperparameter controlling the weight of the sparsity loss, |ℳ|\lvert\mathcal{M}\rvert denotes the total element number of the mask, SS denotes the target sparsity budget, e.g., 50%.

3.3 Inference-time Group Skipping with Unified Mask Reordering

Unlike MoE-style routing, dynamic pruning does not assume a fixed compute budget for each token. A naive implementation therefore typically needs to explicitly convert routing masks into active indices and then use gather-scatter operations to feed only active tokens into GEMM or attention kernels. Let 𝐂=𝐀𝐁⊤\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}^{\top}, where 𝐀∈ℝM×K\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times K}, 𝐁∈ℝN×K\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times K}, and 𝐂∈ℝM×N\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}. This strategy introduces two major sources of overhead:

(1). Device-to-host synchronization. The active token layout must be derived from input-dependent masks before constructing the compact gathered matrix, which can trigger device-to-host synchronization and break CUDA Graph execution.

(2). Extra memory movement and storage. For dynamic depth pruning, ignoring mask and index-processing overhead, explicit gather-scatter increases the memory traffic of a dense GEMM by roughly 3​p​M​(N+K)+N​K+M​NM​K+N​K+M​N\frac{3pM(N+K)+NK+MN}{MK+NK+MN}, where pp denotes the active ratio. For finer-grained dynamic width pruning, each token may select a different subset of 𝐁\mathbf{B}. A naive N-axis implementation therefore incurs traffic of M​K+3​p​M​N​K+3​p​M​N+M​NMK+3pMNK+3pMN+MN, while its K-axis counterpart incurs 3​p​M​K+3​p​M​N​K+M​N3pMK+3pMNK+MN, both require dominant intermediate storage of p​M​N​KpMNK for token-specific weight subsets 𝐁s​u​b\mathbf{B}_{sub} (see Appendix A). As shown in Fig. 3, these non-GEMM overheads are difficult to hide in both prefilling and decoding, while such implementations also struggle with more complex tiled operators such as flash attention (Dao, 2023). WIDE therefore introduces a unified mask-reordering preprocessing step with fused gather-scatter kernels that remain close to the original tile-based pipeline, as illustrated in Fig. 2.

Under this notation, WIDE represents dynamic routing decisions with a binary mask ℳ∈{0,1}M×NG\mathcal{M}\in\{0,1\}^{M\times N_{G}}, where NG=1N_{G}=1 for M-axis routing (i.e., dynamic depth) and NG=Dp/GN_{G}=D_{\text{p}}/G for width pruning over the pruned feature dimension DpD_{\text{p}}. For each group gg, the mask is sorted along the MM dimension, producing a reordered mask ℳ~:,g\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{:,g} and the corresponding row indices ℐ:,g\mathcal{I}_{:,g}:

(ℳ~:,g,ℐ:,g)=SortDesc(ℳ:,g).\displaystyle(\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{:,g},\mathcal{I}_{:,g})=\operatorname{SortDesc}(\mathcal{M}_{:,g}). (7)

Sorting each routing column packs active rows into a contiguous prefix, while ℐ:,g\mathcal{I}_{:,g} gathers the corresponding activation rows and scatters their outputs back. This turns irregular token-wise routing into CTA-level regularity: except for at most one boundary tile per group, CTA row tiles are fully active / inactive. The active row in each admitted GEMM CTA consequently share a group-aligned weight tile 𝐁tile∈ℝB​N×B​K\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{tile}}\in\mathbb{R}^{BN\times BK}, enabling multi-granularity predicated skipping in dense-style tiling and mainloop while avoiding token-specific weight materialization. Based on this layout, WIDE applies a unified skipping predicate over progressively finer row groups. Let

S0=B​M,S1=Sld,S2=Smma,\displaystyle S_{0}=BM,\qquad S_{1}=S_{\text{ld}},\qquad S_{2}=S_{\text{mma}}, (8)

where S0S_{0} is the CTA-level block size, while SldS_{\text{ld}} and SmmaS_{\text{mma}} are architecture-dependent granularities for 𝐀\mathbf{A} loading and MMA execution. For level ℓ∈{0,1,2}\ell\in\{0,1,2\}, group gg, and row block mm, WIDE computes

sm,g(ℓ)=⋁i=m​Sℓmin⁡((m+1)​Sℓ,M)−1ℳ~i,g\displaystyle s^{(\ell)}_{m,g}=\bigvee_{i=mS_{\ell}}^{\min((m+1)S_{\ell},M)-1}\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{i,g} (9)

If sm,g(ℓ)=0s^{(\ell)}_{m,g}=0, the corresponding unit at level ℓ\ell is skipped; otherwise it is executed. This single predicate instantiates three stages: ℓ=0\ell=0 performs hardware-agnostic CTA early exit, ℓ=1\ell=1 skips inactive 𝐀\mathbf{A} load packets, and ℓ=2\ell=2 skips inactive MMA fragments11 1 ℓ∈{1,2}\ell\in\{1,2\} are depended on the GPU architecture, e.g., cp.async vs Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) gather4, and warp-level wmma vs CTA-level wgmma and tcgen05.mma. Under this abstraction, the proposed GEMM-MN, GEMM-K, and Attention kernels cover Q/Up/Gate projections, O/Down projections, and flash attention operations with customized routing group, ensuring WIDE to maximize the acceleration potential brought by sparsity while preserving its vanilla mainloops. The detailed implementation for each kernel is available at Appendix B.

4 Experiments

4.1 Settings

Training

The Llama3.1-8B and Llama3.2-3B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) models are introduced as the backbone model. Unless otherwise specified, all experiments use a subset of RedPajama-1T (Weber et al., 2024)22 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/ZengXiangyu/RedPajama-Data-1T-Sample as the calibration and LoRA recovery corpus. Both training stages are run for 10k steps with batch size 16 and maximum sequence length 4,096, using 4 NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40G GPUs with PyTorch FSDP2. For router training, the Gumbel-Softmax temperature is linearly annealed from 5 to 0.5, and the weight α\alpha is set to 20, following SkipGPT. For LoRA recovery, the LoRA rr and α\alpha is set to 16 and 32, respectively, with additional 0.1 dropout ratio.

Evaluation

We evaluate all models with lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024), using a maximum context length of 4,096. We report perplexity on WikiText2 (Merity et al., 2016) and zero-shot accuracy on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018), BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2021), PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), and HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019). The average accuracy and performance retention ratio is computed over the seven zero-shot classification tasks.

Inference Implementation

For kernel-level throughput evaluation, we use the Triton benchmark interface (Tillet et al., 2019) and report TFLOPs under CUDA Graph replay. For end-to-end acceleration, an ELANA-style profiling tool (Chiang et al., 2025) is introduced to measure single-step Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and Time-Per-Output-Token (TPOT) under CUDA Graph execution. We implement WIDE kernels with both tile-level Domain Specific Languages (DSLs), e.g., Triton (Tillet et al., 2019) and Tilelang (Wang et al., 2025), following a lower-level implementation based on the CuTe template library in CUTLASS together with the TVM-FFI Just-In-Time (JIT) interface used by SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024). The CuTe implementation provides the most fine-grained control and enables intra-block skipping during both 𝐀\mathbf{A} loading and MMA execution, while the tile-level DSL implementations only support CTA-level skipping due to their coarser control granularity. All inference experiments are mainly conducted on GPUs with sm120 architecture (NVIDIA RTX 5090).

Baselines

We compare WIDE with representative static and dynamic pruning methods. For static depth pruning, we include Shortened LLaMA (Kim et al., 2024) and CoopPruner (Ding et al., 2025). For static width pruning, SliceGPT (Ashkboos et al., 2023), Týr-the-Pruner (Li et al., 2025), and DDP (Huang et al., 2026) are included. For dynamic pruning, D-LLM (Jiang et al., 2024) and SkipGPT (Zhao et al., 2025) is selected as the baselines. To ensure fair comparison, all methods use the same RedPajama-1T subset for calibration and LoRA recovery. The calibration stage follows each method’s original training budget, while the LoRA stage uses the same settings as WIDE. For SkipGPT, we additionally increase the router rank rr to match the router capacity of WIDE.

4.2 Main Results

Calibration-only Results

Table 1 compares all methods in the calibration-only setting. Two observations stand out. First, WIDE is already reliable at moderate sparsity. On Llama3.1-8B with 25% sparsity, the G=32G=32 variant retains 97.92% of the dense accuracy, while G=64G=64 still slightly exceeds DDP, the state-of-the-art static width pruning methods (90.68% vs. 89.93%). In contrast, the layer-wise dynamic baseline SkipGPT retains only 72.22%, suggesting that most of the gain comes from moving dynamic routing from layer selection to width allocation. Second, the advantage becomes much clearer in the more aggressive 50% setting. On Llama3.1-8B, WIDE improves over the strongest non-WIDE baseline by 8.80 average-accuracy points (61.84 vs. 53.04). On Llama3.2-3B, the gap is similar at 8.97 points (57.00 vs. 48.03). Notably, these numbers use only router calibration; several WIDE calibration-only results are already beating LoRA baselines in Table 2.

LoRA Results

Table 2 repeats the comparison after applying the same LoRA recovery recipe to every pruned model. The main trend remains unchanged, but the gaps are more informative after recovery. At 25% sparsity on Llama3.1-8B, the choice of group size has little effect: all three WIDE variants retain lossless performance of dense baseline. At 50% sparsity, LoRA narrows the gap for several baselines, especially SkipGPT, yet WIDE still stays around the 90% retention regime on both backbones. Its best configurations reach 64.82 average accuracy on Llama3.1-8B and 58.77 on Llama3.2-3B, improving over SkipGPT by 3.22 and 4.44 points, and over DDP by 10.19 and 9.89 points. The stricter uniform-sparsity and real-sparsity-aligned studies in the Appendix C also points in the same direction.

4.3 Analysis on Pruning Group, Sparsity, and Acceleration

For WIDE, it exposes two knobs that jointly determine the quality–speed trade-off: the group size GG controls routing granularity, while the target sparsity set the computing budget. Their effects, along with the overall acceleration landscape will be analyzed in this section.

The Upper Bound of Speedup

Before analyzing the effects of the other design variables, we quantify the maximum speedup that WIDE can achieve. We record a forward-pass trace on Llama3.1-8B at 50% sparsity with B=1B=1, T=16,384T=16{,}384, and G=128G=128 (Fig. 4). The operations on the accelerated path deliver average speedups of 1.82×1.82\times for prefill and 1.92×1.92\times for decoding, which close to the ideal upper bound. The remaining latency comes from KV projections, element-wise operations, CUDA Graph launches, and WIDE’s own overhead, including router execution and the kernel initialization. These components account for about 16.7% of total prefill latency and 29.1% of total decoding latency, which explains why the layer-wise speedup remains below the theoretical speedup.

Effects of Pruning Group

After the overall acceleration landscape, we then isolate the group size, which trades routing flexibility for kernel efficiency. Table 5 shows that quality is robust across GG, where increasing GffnG_{\text{ffn}} from 16 to 256 at 50% sparsity decreases average accuracy by 2.62 points, and changing GffnG_{\text{ffn}} from 16 to 512 after LoRA tuning only lowers accuracy by 1.13 points, with similar trends at Table 2 and attention side. Figure 7 explains why larger groups are preferable in practice. GEMM-K approaches the ideal speedup only when G>128G>128, as small K-axis groups leave too little mainloop work to amortize pipeline overhead; GEMM-MN also needs G⩾128G\geqslant 128 to preserve a tunable tiling space. Attention kernels are less sensitive, as head-wise pruning largely preserves the original pipeline and remains fast in both long-prefill and decoding regimes, but a GQA-aligned settings are still essential for GQA-packing decoding (Appendix C).

Performance over Sparsity

To examine sensitivity to the pruning budget, we sweep target sparsity from 10% to 70% on Llama3.2-3B and compare WIDE with DDP and SkipGPT, representative static-width and dynamic-depth pruning baselines (Figure 6). WIDE’s average zero-shot accuracy declines gradually across the full range, both before and after LoRA recovery. In contrast, calibration-only SkipGPT drops sharply at 20% sparsity. From 20% to 70%, calibration-only WIDE also remains more accurate than LoRA-recovered SkipGPT. Figure 8 further reports end-to-end throughput across sparsity levels and group sizes. At 0% sparsity, the best setting with G⩽128G\leqslant 128 retains 98.60% of dense throughput, indicating that routing and optimized kernels add little overhead. At 50% sparsity, the best configuration accelerates prefill by 1.68×1.68\times and decode by 1.55×1.55\times. Together, the two curves give a flexible quality–throughput trade-off, where WIDE requires minimal extra cost at low sparsity, and higher sparsity yields more measurable speedups without an abrupt loss of accuracy.

4.4 Routing Behavior

To understand how WIDE allocate its compute budget, we inspect the learned routing patterns at both the layer and token levels. Figure 9 summarizes the routing distribution of the Llama3.1-8B checkpoint with 50% target sparsity and group size 128. Although the overall sparsity is close to the target (47.3%), the learned allocation is highly non-uniform. Attention carries most of the skipping, reaching 66.2% sparsity on WikiText2, while the FFN is more conservative at 28.5%. Across layers, both curves peak around layers 4–12 and 24–28, and dip near the model boundaries and layers 15–18.

These profiles echo the layer sensitivity observed in static pruning studies (He et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2026), but are produced here by token-conditioned group routing. For the token-wise routing behavior, Figure 10 shows a representative case study on HellaSwag. In here, he FFN routers keep semantic content tokens such as boy, running, and track, especially in layers 9–11 where the average FFN sparsity is high, while articles like A, a, and the are often skipped. Similar behavior appears in the appendix cases across other tasks (Fig 14 to Fig 18). This analysis highlight the ability that WIDE can dynamically allocate its budget across layer and tokens with semantic-awareness.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we identify the potential limitation for current naive token-wise dynamic pruning pipeline under modern high-throughput inference system, and present a finer-grained group-based dynamic width pruning baseline with unified acceleration design for routing-based dynamic structural pruning. The presented WIDE uses lightweight bottleneck routers and differentiable masks to select GQA head groups and FFN parameter groups for each token, pushing structured pruning below the granularity of layers and sublayers. In the system side, we formulate mask-based dynamic pruning as two steps: mask reordering and progressive intra-kernel skipping. This abstraction lets the same routing decisions be consumed by customized attention and GEMM kernels with limited disruption to dense execution. Across calibration-only and LoRA-recovered settings, WIDE improves the quality-sparsity trade-off over existing structured static and dynamic pruning methods, while its kernels translate the learned sparsity into practical speedups under CUDA Graph execution for both batched prefill and decode workloads. These results suggest that fine-grained dynamic pruning needs to be designed together with the hardware execution path, rather than treated as a model-only compression problem.

Appendix A The Cost for Naive Gather-Scatter Implementations

In this section, we first provide a narrow, theoretical memory accounting for naive gather-scatter implementations of M-axis, N-axis, and K-axis dynamic pruning. We count logical data-element transfers caused by materializing and consuming the explicit data tensors in the PyTorch-style implementations below. Routing masks, indices, offsets, and their construction, storage, and traffic are excluded, as are hardware-specific cache effects, and framework workspace. We assume that 𝐀\mathbf{A}, 𝐁\mathbf{B}, and 𝐂\mathbf{C} use the same data type, so byte traffic is obtained by multiplying TMT_{M}, TNT_{N}, or TKT_{K} by the data-type size. Consider a dense GEMM

C=AB⊤,A∈ℝM×K,B∈ℝN×K,C∈ℝM×N\displaystyle\textbf{C}=\textbf{A}\textbf{B}^{\top},\qquad\textbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times K},\quad\textbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times K},\quad\textbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N} (10)

The ideal dense traffic is

Tdense≈M​K+N​K+M​N\displaystyle T_{\text{dense}}\approx MK+NK+MN (11)

which corresponding to reading A, reading B, and writing C.

Naive M-axis pruning.

M-axis pruning (i.e., dynamic depth pruning) selects a subset of token rows for the current operator. Let M′=p​MM^{\prime}=pM be the number of active rows, where pp is the active ratio, and let IM∈ℤM′I_{M}\in\mathbb{Z}^{M^{\prime}} denote the active row indices. A naive PyTorch-style implementation gathers active rows, computes the compact GEMM, and scatters the result back like:

⬇
# A: [M, K]
# B: [N, K]
# I_M: [M’]
A_sub = A[I_M, :] # [M’, K]
C_sub = A_sub @ B.T # [M’, N]
C = torch.zeros(M, N, device=A.device, dtype=A.dtype)
C[I_M, :] = C_sub # scatter back to dense output

When ignoring index traffic, the total memory traffic is

TM\displaystyle T_{M} ≈3​M′​K+N​K+3​M′​N+M​N\displaystyle\approx 3M^{\prime}K+NK+3M^{\prime}N+MN
=3​p​M​K+N​K+3​p​M​N+M​N\displaystyle=3pMK+NK+3pMN+MN (12)

The terms 3​M′​K3M^{\prime}K and 3​M′​N3M^{\prime}N come from materializing and rereading Asub\textbf{A}_{\text{sub}} and Csub\textbf{C}_{\text{sub}}, respectively, while M​NMN comes from initializing the dense output tensor. The additional storage, excluding the final dense output C, is

SM\displaystyle S_{M} ≈M′​K+M′​N\displaystyle\approx M^{\prime}K+M^{\prime}N
=p​M​K+p​M​N\displaystyle=pMK+pMN (13)

Naive N-axis pruning.

N-axis pruning selects different NN-axis groups for each token. Divide the NN-axis into groups of size GG. If each token selects RR groups, the active NN-axis extent is

N′=R​G=p​N\displaystyle N^{\prime}=RG=pN (14)

where pp is the active ratio along the NN-axis. Let IN∈ℤM×RI_{N}\in\mathbb{Z}^{M\times R} be the per-token selected group indices. The fully vectorized PyTorch-style implementation below first expands group indices and materializes token-specific subsets of BB:

⬇
# A: [M, K]
# B: [N, K]
# I_N: [M, R], group indices
# G: group size
# N_prime = R * G
offset = torch.arange(G, device=A.device) # [G]
J_N = I_N[..., None] * G + offset # [M, R, G]
J_N = J_N.reshape(M, R * G) # [M, N’]
B_sub = B[J_N, :] # [M, N’, K]
C_sub = torch.einsum("mk,mnk->mn", A, B_sub) # [M, N’]
C = torch.zeros(M, N, device=A.device, dtype=A.dtype)
C.scatter_(dim=1, index=J_N, src=C_sub) # [M, N]

Ignoring index traffic and the small offset tensor, the overall memory traffic is

TN\displaystyle T_{N} ≈M​K+3​M​N′​K+3​M​N′+M​N\displaystyle\approx MK+3MN^{\prime}K+3MN^{\prime}+MN
=M​K+3​p​M​N​K+3​p​M​N+M​N\displaystyle=MK+3pMNK+3pMN+MN (15)

The dominant term 3​M​N′​K3MN^{\prime}K comes from reading selected rows of B, writing the gathered tensor Bsub\textbf{B}_{\text{sub}}, and reading Bsub\textbf{B}_{\text{sub}} again during token-wise dot products. Unlike dense GEMM, where B is shared across all MM rows and read once as N​KNK, the naive N-axis implementation replicates selected weight groups for each token. The additional storage is

SN\displaystyle S_{N} ≈M​N′​K+M​N′\displaystyle\approx MN^{\prime}K+MN^{\prime}
=p​M​N​K+p​M​N\displaystyle=pMNK+pMN (16)

which is dominated by the per-token gathered weight tensor Bsub∈ℝM×N′×K\textbf{B}_{\text{sub}}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N^{\prime}\times K}, where the remaining M​N′MN^{\prime} entries belong to Csub\textbf{C}_{\text{sub}}.

Naive K-axis pruning.

For attention output and FFN down projections, K-axis pruning is applied over the reduction dimension KK. Divide the KK-axis into groups of size GG. If each token selects RR groups, the active KK-axis extent is

K′=R​G=p​K\displaystyle K^{\prime}=RG=pK (17)

where pp is the active ratio along the KK-axis. Let IK∈ℤM×RI_{K}\in\mathbb{Z}^{M\times R} denote the per-token selected KK-group indices. A token-specific PyTorch-style implementation can be written as:

⬇
# A: [M, K]
# B: [N, K]
# I_K: [M, R], group indices
# G: group size
# K_prime = R * G
offset = torch.arange(G, device=A.device) # [G]
J_K = I_K[..., None] * G + offset # [M, R, G]
J_K = J_K.reshape(M, R * G) # [M, K’]
A_sub = torch.gather(A, dim=1, index=J_K) # [M, K’]
B_sub = B[:, J_K].permute(1, 0, 2) # [M, N, K’]
C = torch.einsum("mk,mnk->mn", A_sub, B_sub) # [M, N]

Ignoring index traffic and the small offset tensor, the total memory traffic is

TK\displaystyle T_{K} ≈3​M​K′+3​M​N​K′+M​N\displaystyle\approx 3MK^{\prime}+3MNK^{\prime}+MN
=3​p​M​K+3​p​M​N​K+M​N\displaystyle=3pMK+3pMNK+MN (18)

The term 3​M​K′3MK^{\prime} comes from reading selected entries of 𝐀\mathbf{A}, writing 𝐀sub\mathbf{A}_{\text{sub}}, and reading 𝐀sub\mathbf{A}_{\text{sub}} again during the token-wise dot product. The dominant term 3​M​N​K′3MNK^{\prime} comes from reading selected entries of 𝐁\mathbf{B}, writing the token-specific tensor 𝐁sub\mathbf{B}_{\text{sub}}, and reading 𝐁sub\mathbf{B}_{\text{sub}} again during the einsum. The additional materialized data-tensor storage is

SK\displaystyle S_{K} ≈M​N​K′+M​K′\displaystyle\approx MNK^{\prime}+MK^{\prime}
=p​M​N​K+p​M​K\displaystyle=pMNK+pMK (19)

which is dominated by the token-specific gathered weight tensor 𝐁sub∈ℝM×N×K′\mathbf{B}_{\text{sub}}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N\times K^{\prime}}, where the remaining M​K′MK^{\prime} entries belong to 𝐀sub\mathbf{A}_{\text{sub}}.

These estimates highlight why the fully vectorized N-axis and K-axis implementations above are especially inefficient: they materialize token-specific subsets of B, incurring O⁡(p​M​N​K)O(pMNK) intermediate storage and destroying the regular weight reuse of dense GEMM, which highlight the role of customized fuse kernel. The results are summarized in Table 3.

Building on the theoretical analysis, we further benchmark the throughput and peak memory usage of the dense GEMM baseline, naive gather-scatter kernel, and optimized CuTe GEMM kernel for pruning along the M, N, and K axes. Since the naive implementation can be compatible with grouped-GEMM by mask-reordering preprocessing, we also introduce it as a stronger baseline. The results are shown in Figure 11. For the coarsest-grained M-axis pruning setting, the explicit gather-scatter kernel still delivers a meaningful speedup but incurs an additional memory overhead of roughly 2x. For the finer-grained GEMM-N and GEMM-K settings, however, the naive implementation is constrained by the massive additional memory traffic, achieving only about 1.0 TFLOPS and requiring roughly 1,000x the memory footprint, where the optimized grouped-GEMM kernel still requires 20x more memory footprint and only achieves 50∼\sim100 TFLOPS, failing to reach the dense GEMM baseline. In contrast, the fused CuTe kernel incurs virtually no additional memory-storage overhead and can already deliver speedups for matrix of size 204832048^{3}.

Appendix B CuTe Kernel Details

At the abstraction level, all three CuTe kernels follow the same execution path as the framework in the main text: (1) standalone mask-reordering preprocessing, (2) hardware-agnostic block-level skipping at stage ℓ=0\ell=0, (3) a dense-style tiled pipeline with optional hardware-dependent intra-block skipping during operand gathering (ℓ=1\ell=1, corresponding to 𝐀\mathbf{A} loading in GEMM and 𝐐\mathbf{Q} loading in attention) and MMA execution (ℓ=2\ell=2), and finally, (4) a scatter epilogue. The latter two predicates are enabled only when selected by the architecture-specific kernel configuration.

Herein, we first describe the metadata shared by all three kernels. A routing column is ℳ:,g\mathcal{M}_{:,g} after flattening the batch and token dimensions for GEMM, and ℳb,:,g\mathcal{M}_{b,:,g} for flash attention. As summarized in Algorithm 1, each routing column is sorted independently on the GPU. In this way, the resulting index ℐj,g\mathcal{I}_{j,g} maps logical row jj back to its physical row, i.e., ℳ~j,g=ℳℐj,g,g\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{j,g}=\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{I}_{j,g},g}. Activation tensors therefore remain in their original layout and are gathered/scattered directly through the reordered indices. Consecutive operators governed by the same routing decision can reuse this metadata, although zero initialization remains necessary for skipped blocks and atomic-add epilogues.

For a sorted CTA row tile ℛ0=[m0,min⁡(m0+B​M,M))\mathcal{R}_{0}=[m_{0},\min(m_{0}+BM,M)), the block-level predicate is simply s(0)=ℳ~m0,gs^{(0)}=\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{m_{0},g}. Because the column is monotone, s(0)=0s^{(0)}=0 proves that the whole CTA and every later CTA for this group are inactive. Conversely, if a full tile’s last entry is active, the kernel takes an all-active fast path and avoids loading per-row masks. For a load packet uu spanning SldS_{\mathrm{ld}} rows and an MMA row fragment vv spanning SmmaS_{\mathrm{mma}} rows, the finer predicates are

su(1)\displaystyle s^{(1)}_{u} =⋁j∈ℛld​(u)ℳ~j,g,\displaystyle=\bigvee_{j\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ld}}(u)}\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{j,g}, sv(2)\displaystyle s^{(2)}_{v} =⋁j∈ℛmma​(v)ℳ~j,g.\displaystyle=\bigvee_{j\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{mma}}(v)}\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{j,g}. (20)

The ℓ=1\ell=1 predicate is instantiated per thread or per warp according to the CuTe copy atom. The ℓ=2\ell=2 predicate is reduced with a warp vote instruction and therefore keeps uniform across all lanes issuing the same tensor-core instruction. In the pseudocode below, Predicates returns (s(0),s(1),s(2),𝒥)(s^{(0)},s^{(1)},s^{(2)},\mathcal{J}), where 𝒥\mathcal{J} contains the original row indices needed by the active packets. We omit CuTe layout construction, register-fragment permutations, and architecture-specific barrier phases that do not change the execution schedule. PrefetchMN and PrefetchK denote semantic producer operations: they conditionally gather active 𝐀\mathbf{A} packets according to s(1)s^{(1)}, stage the dense 𝐁\mathbf{B} tile, and commit one stage. WaitStage and ReleaseStage denote the corresponding consumer operations.

Implementation of GEMM-MN

GEMM-MN is the shared kernel for M-axis and N-axis pruning. Its N-axis path applies routing to the attention Q and FFN up/gate projections, while M-axis dynamic depth pruning is the NG=1N_{G}=1 special case of the same execution path. Let 𝐂=𝐀𝐁⊤\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}^{\top}, with 𝐀∈ℝM×K\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times K} and 𝐁∈ℝN×K\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times K}, and partition NN into groups of width GG. Each CTA owns one (B​M,B​N)(BM,BN) output tile, so its NN coordinate uniquely selects a routing group gg that is selected by B​MBM tokens. Algorithm 2 makes the CTA admission, prologue, pipelined mainloop, and epilogue path explicit.

The important pipeline invariant is that each logical KK tile still commits exactly one asynchronous-copy group: sparse predicates suppress only 𝐀\mathbf{A} load packets, while the dense 𝐁\mathbf{B} copy keeps the producer stage well-defined. Split-KK variants use the same mainloop and atomically reduce the scattered partial outputs. For the GEMV (General Matrix-Vector Multiplication) variant, it can be dispatched in M⩽4M\leqslant 4.

Implementation of GEMM-K

GEMM-K implements the K-axis path for the attention output and FFN down projections. Here the routed dimension is the reduction dimension:

𝐂m,n=∑g=0NG−1ℳm,g​∑k∈𝒦g𝐀m,k​𝐁n,k,|𝒦g|=G.\displaystyle\mathbf{C}_{m,n}=\sum_{g=0}^{N_{G}-1}\mathcal{M}_{m,g}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{g}}\mathbf{A}_{m,k}\mathbf{B}_{n,k},\qquad|\mathcal{K}_{g}|=G. (21)

Because different groups have different row permutations, each active group computes a partial output and scatters it with an atomic reduction, as shown in Algorithm 3.

Unlike GEMM-MN, GEMM-K scopes its pipeline to one active KK-group. The producer–consumer ring and accumulator reset at each group boundary, while an inactive group skips its copies, synchronizations, MMA, and epilogue work entirely. This group-local design sacrifices prefetching across adjacent KK-groups, but allows ℓ=0\ell=0 block-level skipping to bypass the entire inner pipeline. Advancing a shared ring over skipped groups would otherwise leave unmatched wait/commit operations and increase barrier-management overhead. It also creates substantial atomic-reduction contention because around ⌈K/G⌉\lceil K/G\rceil groups may scatter partial outputs to the same entries of 𝐂\mathbf{C}. We mitigate this contention with an outer loop that packs multiple KK-groups into one CTA and executes them sequentially, thus reducing concurrent writebacks. For the GEMV variant in GEMM-K, it can be dispatched in M=1M=1, and M∈{2,3,4}M\in\{2,3,4\} for G⩾256G\geqslant 256.

On sm90+, TMA also supports asynchronous tensor reduction from shared to global memory through cp.reduce.async.bulk.tensor. This enables atomic writeback from shared memory, allowing a warp-specialized pipeline to overlap the atomic epilogue with the mainloop and potentially improve GEMM-K performance for small GG. This optimization is less suitable for sm120: persistently storing 𝐂\mathbf{C} in shared memory consumes too much of the limited shared-memory capacity and substantially reduces occupancy. We therefore leave it as future work.

Implementation of Attention

For prefilling, a CTA owns a partial tiles query at batch bb and head hqh_{q}. The query head determines both its KV head for GQA and routing group gg. Algorithm 4 follows the tiled online-softmax organization of FlashAttention (Dao, 2023), while fusing the same three predicates into the query-side work. Its path is query-tile admission, 𝐐\mathbf{Q} prologue, dense 𝐊/𝐕\mathbf{K}/\mathbf{V} pipelined mainloop, and scatter epilogue. Here OnlineSoftmax updates (𝐦,𝐳,𝐎acc)(\mathbf{m},\mathbf{z},\mathbf{O}_{\mathrm{acc}}) only for active rows and returns 𝐏\mathbf{P}, where a fully masked row returns 𝐏[r,:]=𝟎\mathbf{P}[r,:]=\mathbf{0} and leaves its running state unchanged.

Once a CTA is admitted, KK and VV remain dense and their two producer–consumer pipelines advance once per logical key tile. Row-level predicates never suppress a barrier arrival or stage transition. They only suppress the gathered QQ packets and the QK/PV MMA fragments, preserving barrier phase agreement across the CTA. For causal attention, the streamed KV range is shortened using the maximum aligned active query position 𝒥+δ\mathcal{J}+\delta. A streamed tile wholly inside the valid range and ending no later than the minimum aligned query position takes a fully-valid fast path; only boundary tiles evaluate element-wise causal predicates. For decoding (Tq=1T_{q}=1), mask reordering is bypassed and routing is checked directly at the block level, while the split online-softmax pipeline follows the same abstraction, similar to the GEMV variants of GEMM-MN and GEMM-K.

Appendix C Additional Experimental Results

Benchmark over Uniform Sparsity

We further evaluate WIDE with a uniform sparsity constraint that allocates the pruning budget equally between the attention and FFN modules. Specifically, we decompose the sparsity loss into separate attention and FFN terms:

ℒ=ℒLM+α2​(|S−1N​∑i=1N(1−∑ℳattni|ℳattni|)|+|S−1N​∑i=1N(1−∑ℳffni|ℳffni|)|)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}+\frac{\alpha}{2}\Bigg(\left\lvert S-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(1-\frac{\sum\mathcal{M}_{\text{attn}}^{i}}{\lvert\mathcal{M}_{\text{attn}}^{i}\rvert}\right)\right\rvert+\left\lvert S-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(1-\frac{\sum\mathcal{M}_{\text{ffn}}^{i}}{\lvert\mathcal{M}_{\text{ffn}}^{i}\rvert}\right)\right\rvert\Bigg) (22)

This design constrains the sparsity of the two modules independently rather than matching only their average, keeping their module-wise sparsity levels close to a 1:1 ratio. As shown in Table 4, the uniform constraint causes a larger accuracy drop at larger group sizes, but LoRA recovery restores most of the lost accuracy. After recovery, the uniform variant is within roughly 4% of the unconstrained WIDE variant and still significantly outperforms static structured pruning at the same budget. The layer-wise sparsity profiles in Fig. 12 support the same interpretation: enforcing uniformity between attention and FFN does not alter how sparsity is distributed across layers, it only shifts the profile without changing its shape. Thus, the allocation learned by WIDE appears to capture a stable layer-importance pattern induced by the router, suggesting that the router learns a locally optimal allocation for the provided data distribution.

Here are the full results for Llama3.1-8B and Llama3.2-3B (Table 5, 6, and 7).

Decoding Speedup for Different Attention Group Size

Figure 13 shows how the attention group size affects decoding. In Gattn⩽HqHk×dG_{\text{attn}}\leqslant\frac{H_{q}}{H_{k}}\times d, the kernel progressively transitions from vanilla multi-head attention to GQA-packing attention, where a single CTA partition can read and compute at most HqHk\frac{H_{q}}{H_{k}} heads in parallel. Increasing GattnG_{\text{attn}} beyond this threshold does not affect the tiling strategy used for attention decoding.

Full Visualization Results on Routing Decision

Figures 14 to 18 provide additional visualizations of WIDE’s token-wise routing decisions and reveal the same semantic-aware behavior in Figure 10. Figure 19 further compares the probability of retaining each routing group across low and high sparsity layers in the attention and FFN modules, where the patterns are differing across layers.
